title: why people stand up when the book comes in
hook: why people stand up when the book comes in

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sign of the cross: forehead, chest, one shoulder, the other. Your line was: head, heart, shoulders — all of you. Which one was carrying the most? Day three.

If you've ever been to a Catholic Mass as a guest, you know the feeling. Everyone else seems to know when to sit, when to stand, when to kneel, and you're half a second behind, watching the person in front of you. There's one moment that catches visitors most. People have been sitting quietly, listening to readings. Then music starts, often the word alleluia, and the whole room stands up at once. Someone at the front lifts a book up high. Why stand for a book? For the next three days we're going to walk through the Mass like a play in three scenes. Today, scene one: the story.
screen: `SIT, STAND, KNEEL.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM STANDS.` → `SCENE ONE: THE STORY.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Mass comes from the old Latin ending of the service, ite, missa est, roughly: go, you are sent. So the whole thing is named for the moment you walk back out the door. Now, scene one. Catholics call it the Liturgy of the Word, and it's mostly listening. On a Sunday there's usually a reading from the Old Testament, then a psalm, often sung back and forth, then a reading from one of the letters of the apostles. People sit for those. Then comes the Gospel, one of the four books about the life of Jesus, and everyone stands. Gospel is an old English word, good news, for the Greek euangelion. Catholics say that when the Gospel is read, Christ himself is speaking to the people gathered there. So you stand the way you'd stand when someone important walks into the room. There's a small ritual right before it, too. Many people trace three little crosses with their thumb: on the forehead, on the lips, on the heart. Remember yesterday's sign? It's the same idea, shrunk down. The words be in my mind, on my lips, in my heart. Standing for the book isn't new, either. The Bible itself describes it. In the book of Nehemiah, after the exile, the scribe Ezra opens the book of the law in front of the whole people, and when he opens it, they all stand up. And in Luke's Gospel, when Jesus goes home to Nazareth, he goes to the synagogue and stands up to read the scroll of Isaiah. People have been rising for the reading for a very long time. Then everyone sits again, and a priest or deacon preaches: the homily. The story has entered the room, and scene one ends.
screen: `MASS — GO, YOU ARE SENT.` · `READINGS, A PSALM, THEN THE GOSPEL.` · `THREE SMALL CROSSES.` · `EZRA OPENS THE BOOK. THEY STAND.` · then, large: `THE STORY ENTERS THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Three breaths, with the bell. If you're sitting, stand up, just for this, the way the room stands for the Gospel. On the first breath, touch your forehead. On the second, your lips. On the third, your heart. You don't have to say anything. Just let each place get ready to listen.
The Gospel. The good news: the reading about the life of Jesus that everyone stands to hear, the high point of scene one of the Mass. Third word.
Your line: the story enters the room. Today, when someone starts telling you something that matters to them, give it the full attention of a room standing up. Day three.

howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics sit for the first readings and the psalm, then stand for the Gospel, often tracing small crosses on the forehead, lips and heart as it is announced.

fork.setup: you're in the crowd when the scribe Ezra lifts the book of the law and opens it in front of everyone. what do the people do?
options: they cover their faces and sit.
fork.reveal: when he opened the book, all the people stood. Catholics still stand for the Gospel, a habit thousands of years old.

original.note: Latin: go, you are sent (literally, it is the sending). the dismissal that gave the Mass its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: church people just stand up and sit down a lot.
what it means: scene one of the Mass is the story, and people stand for the Gospel because Catholics say Christ speaks in it.
what a scholar hears: standing for the reading goes back to Ezra in Nehemiah 8; the name Mass comes from the dismissal, ite, missa est.

sources.ref: General Instruction of the Roman Missal, on the Liturgy of the Word

notes: Sunday pattern: Old Testament reading, responsorial psalm, New Testament reading, Gospel; confirm (in Easter season the first reading is usually from Acts).
Three small crosses on forehead, lips and heart: the voice gives a common meaning ('in my mind, on my lips, in my heart'); this is a popular explanation, not a fixed text. Confirm wording.
'Christ himself is speaking' paraphrases Catholic teaching on Christ's presence in the word proclaimed (Sacrosanctum Concilium 7). Confirm.
Derivation of Mass from 'ite, missa est' is the standard account; confirm the gloss 'go, you are sent'.
Nehemiah is 2 Esdras in the Douay-Rheims; paraphrased.
